crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in an investment firm maps where artificial intelligence and machine learning are used across the investment lifecycle, from research and portfolio construction to trading, operations, compliance and client reporting.

children.name: Fair Lending and Bias Testing
children.blurb: Fair lending and bias testing covers how lenders and credit decision systems evaluate applicants without unlawful disparate treatment or disparate impact on protected characteristics such as race, national origin, sex, marital status, age, or receipt of public assistance.

children.name: Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients
children.blurb: Explaining models to regulators and clients covers the practice of translating how a model works, what data it uses, and what its outputs mean into language that a non-specialist can act on.

children.name: Protecting Material Non-Public Information
children.blurb: Protecting material non-public information in AI-related firms covers the handling of confidential data about models, training runs, partnerships, regulatory findings, and financial results before public disclosure.

children.name: Verifying What a Model Produced
children.blurb: Verifying what a model produced covers the practices used to confirm that an AI system's outputs are accurate, consistent with their inputs, and fit for the purpose a firm assigns them.

sections.body: Governance and fiduciary risk is the practical work of proving that an AI system inside a financial firm is allowed to run, does not break lending or securities rules, and can be explained when a regulator asks. In investment firms today, AI is being used to scan model inventories against internal policy, run statistical tests on credit decisions for protected classes, and generate plain language summaries of model logic for compliance staff. Data loss prevention tools now inspect prompts and outputs for material non-public information before they leave a firm. Output verification systems log model versions, inputs, and generated text so an auditor can reconstruct what a model produced and when. This is not theoretical oversight; it is daily checking, testing, and record keeping.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has working methods for some narrow tasks, but no general solution. Fair lending testing is well established for traditional scorecards, yet applying the same tests to large language models or deep learning underwriting remains unsettled because those models change behavior with small prompt or data shifts. Explaining models to regulators is solved only for simple models like linear regression or decision trees; for complex models, firms can often describe inputs and outputs but not the internal reasoning in a way that satisfies every examiner. Data loss prevention can catch known patterns such as ticker symbols or deal code words, but it misses paraphrased or indirect leaks. Verifying what a model produced is possible when logging is built in from the start, but retrofitting logs onto existing systems is expensive and often incomplete.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms, which sets out how a firm decides whether a model is safe to deploy and what evidence it must keep. Fair Lending and Bias Testing then narrows the focus to credit and pricing decisions, showing the specific statistical checks that regulators expect. Explaining Models to Regulators and Clients moves from testing to communication, covering the written and verbal explanations a firm must produce. Protecting Material Non-Public Information addresses the leakage risk that arises when employees use AI tools with sensitive deal or portfolio data. Finally, Verifying What a Model Produced closes the loop by describing the logs and audit trails needed to prove what happened after a model ran. Together these pages follow the life of a model from approval to testing, explanation, data handling, and post hoc verification.
